post_title: Cap rate is NOT your return. Cap rate vs cash-on-cash, in plain English.

lines.voice: Cap rate is not your return. Here's the difference, in plain English.
First, {N O I|NOI}. *Rent* comes in. *Taxes*, *insurance*, *repairs* and *vacancy* go out. What's *left* is {N O I|NOI}: what the house earns before any mortgage.
Cap rate is that {N O I|NOI} divided by the price. It's your return if you paid all *cash*. Think of it as the property's *grade*.
But most people borrow. The *bank* takes its mortgage out of that {N O I|NOI}, and what's left is your *cash* flow.
Divide that by the cash you put in, and you get cash-on-cash. Same house: paid in cash, it returns {six and a half percent|6.5%}. With this loan, you get {one point eight|1.8%}.

caption:
Cap rate is NOT your return. Here's the difference, in plain English.

NOI (net operating income): rent minus taxes, insurance, repairs and vacancy. What the house earns before any mortgage.

Cap rate = NOI ÷ price. Your return if you paid all cash. Think of it as the property's grade.
$19,500 ÷ $300,000 = 6.5%

Cash-on-cash = what's left after the mortgage ÷ the cash you actually put in. Your return on YOUR money.
With 25% down at 7%: $1,536 ÷ $84,000 = 1.8%

Cap rate grades the property. Cash-on-cash grades your deal. Check both.
